Gittites
GIT-ites
n. pl.
Inhabitants of Gath, one of the five Philistine cities; Hebrew Gitti. Gath means a winepress. The word covers Goliath, the six hundred men who followed David out of Jerusalem, and Obededom in whose house the ark rested three months and was blessed.

Biblical Definition

The Gittites are men of Gath, and Scripture uses them to show that no nation is beyond the reach of grace. Gath produced Goliath, whose brother… the Gittite Elhanan afterward slew (2 Samuel 21:19). Gath sheltered David twice in his exile. And Gath supplied two of the most striking figures in the David narrative. When the ark struck Uzzah and David feared to bring it further, he turned it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite, and it remained there three months, and the LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household (2 Samuel 6:11) — the ark that killed an Israelite for irreverence blessing a Philistine household for reverence. Then, on the day David fled from Absalom, six hundred Gittites marched with him, and the king tried to send their captain home: Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile (2 Samuel 15:19). Ittai’s answer is one of the great confessions of loyalty in Scripture: as the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be. A Philistine, newly come, chose the rejected king when Israel’s own men chose Absalom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no GITTITE entry. Gath is Hebrew for a winepress, and the gentilic denotes its inhabitants; the Authorized Version also uses Gittith in three psalm titles, probably an instrument or tune of Gath.

GITTITE, n. — An inhabitant of Gath, one of the five lordships of the Philistines.

Hebrew gath signifies a winepress, a common element in Palestinian place names (Gathhepher, Gathrimmon).

The psalm titles of Psalms 8, 81, and 84 read upon Gittith, generally taken as an instrument or melody associated with Gath.

Six hundred Gittites followed David from Gath and formed part of his guard alongside the Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Samuel 15:18).

Webster 1828 does not carry the word; the sense comes from Joshua 13:3 and the books of Samuel.

Key Scripture

Joshua 13:3 — "From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites:"

2 Samuel 6:11 — "And the ark of the LORD continued in the house of Obededom the Gittite three months: and the LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household."

2 Samuel 15:19 — "Then said the king to Ittai the Gittite, Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile."

2 Samuel 15:21 — "And Ittai answered the king, and said, As the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be."

2 Samuel 15:22 — "And David said to Ittai, Go and pass over. And Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him."

Modern Corruption

Ittai’s oath is the plainest picture in the Old Testament of what it costs to follow a rejected king, and it is the exact opposite of the modern gospel invitation that promises the believer the winning side.

expand to see more

David offered Ittai every reason to leave: he was a stranger, an exile, newly come, and the throne was going the other way. Ittai swore by the LORD and by the king that he would be wherever the king was, in death or life, and took his men and his little ones over the brook Kidron with him. Our Lord crossed that same brook on the night He was betrayed, and He had already told the multitudes to count the cost, to hate father and mother in comparison, and to take up the cross. A church that recruits by promising cultural respectability and personal flourishing is not preaching the terms David laid before Ittai, nor the terms Christ laid before the crowd. The convert who understands the offer is the one who says whether in death or life.

The Obededom narrative teaches the complementary point. The ark had just killed Uzzah for steadying it with his hand, and David was afraid of it. Into a Gittite’s house it went, and for three months that household was blessed — so plainly that the report of it drew David back to fetch the ark properly, with Levites bearing it as the law prescribed. The same presence of God is death to presumption and blessing to reverence, and the difference is not nationality. It never was. To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Gath (H1661), a winepress; Gitti (H1663), Gittite; the Gittith (H1665) of three psalm titles is probably an instrument or tune of Gath.

expand to see more

Hebrew gath (H1660) — a winepress; the common noun behind the city name.

Hebrew Gath (H1661) — Gath; one of the five Philistine lordships, Goliath’s city.

Hebrew Gitti (H1663) — Gittite; used of Obededom, of Ittai, and of Goliath’s brother.

Hebrew Gittith (H1665) — the superscription of Psalms 8, 81, and 84, upon Gittith.

Hebrew Obed Edom (H5654) — Obededom, servant of Edom; his house was blessed while the ark lodged there (2 Samuel 6:11).

Usage

"The LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household (2 Samuel 6:11) — the ark that slew Uzzah blessing a Gittite’s house."

"Thou art a stranger, and also an exile (2 Samuel 15:19) — every reason Ittai had to go home."

"Whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be (2 Samuel 15:21) — the answer of a Philistine to a fleeing king."
